The Arab Kings.
Now when al-Muqtadir perceived the rebellion, he was afraid,
and sent to Mu'nis,
saying: "You set me up,
and you have oaths with me.
Therefore, let your mind be reconciled.
I swear by God
that I do not reckon any offense against you.
And if there is something else in your heart,
I take refuge in God,
and never will I contemplate war with you."
Mu'nis, however, would not yield to reconciliation,
but sent and brought the Caliph to him by force,
and imprisoned him in a house.
And he brought Muhammad, the son of al-Mu'tadid, out of prison,
swore allegiance to him, surnamed him al-Qahir,
and sent and seated him upon the throne.
Now when the people of the palace saw that they were being dismissed,
and others were entering into their places,
they drew their swords and killed the nobles who were with al-Qahir,
except for Mu'nis, who was in his own house.
And they seized al-Qahir,
and cried out with a loud voice:
"Long live King al-Muqtadir!"
And they went out from the palace,
and the people of the city joined them,
and they went to the house of Mu'nis.
And they brought out al-Muqtadir,
and brought him back to the palace.
Against Mu'nis, however, they were not able to lay a hand,
because he was greatly feared by all of them.
Then al-Muqtadir sent again to Mu'nis,
and requested of him that he make peace.
He, however, since he did not trust him,
went up hastily to Mosul.
And he gathered his forces there,
and came down again to Baghdad.
Al-Muqtadir also gathered forces and went out and met Mu'nis;
and he was defeated, and the Caliph al-Muqtadir was killed,
and his head was hung on the point of a spear, in the year 320
320 of the Arabs [932 AD].
And in his time was Sinan, the chief of physicians, the son of Thabit of Harran;
and without his permission no one was allowed to practice medicine in Baghdad.
And among the famous stories about him is this:
One day an old physician of handsome appearance came to him,
and Sinan arose and honored him according to his outward appearance.
